Stationarity Test Results (ADF)

The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test checks whether a sensor's statistical properties (mean, variance) stay stable over time. A stationary series (p < 0.05) is well-suited for direct time-series modelling without differencing.

1.

Missing Value Analysis

sensor_15 was 100% null and dropped. sensor_50 is missing 35% of readings (~77,000 minutes). All gaps were filled using forward-fill then back-fill (limit = 30 min) — carrying the last known value forward rather than imputing with mean or zero, which would be physically incorrect for sensor data.

2.

Machine Status Timeline

The machine was NORMAL 93.4% of the time, RECOVERING 6.6%, and BROKEN only 7 times in 5 months (0.003%). The dataset is severely imbalanced — BROKEN events are too rare to learn from directly, making RECOVERING the practical proxy label for a predictive maintenance classifier.

3.

Top-6 Sensor Readings Over Time

Sensors ranked by variance: sensor_28, sensor_23, sensor_36, sensor_31, sensor_32, sensor_26. These carry the most information. Red vertical lines mark the 7 BROKEN events — you can see corresponding spikes or drops in several sensors, confirming they respond to machine state changes.

4.

Seasonal Decomposition — sensor_00

sensor_00's signal is split into Trend (slow drift from 0.02 → 2.52 over 5 months, possibly wear or increasing load), Seasonal (amplitude = 0.05, small daily cycle), and Residual (std = 0.18 — unexplained spikes are where anomalies hide).

5.

Autocorrelation (ACF & PACF)

The ACF decays slowly over 72 hours — the sensor has strong memory. What happened 10 hours ago still influences the current reading. The PACF cuts off sharply, suggesting an AR(1) or AR(2) process is a suitable model. Practically: the next reading is strongly predicted by recent past values.

6.

Rolling Mean & Standard Deviation

24-hour rolling mean and ±2σ band for sensor_00. When the band widens, the sensor is behaving erratically — even if no BROKEN status is yet logged. This widening is a practical early-warning signal: volatility increases before visible failure.

7.

KDE Distributions by Machine Status

For each top-6 sensor, three curves are plotted — one per status. If the machine status had no effect, all curves would overlap. The visible shift between NORMAL and RECOVERING/BROKEN curves confirms that sensors carry real health signal and can power a classification model.

8.

Sensor Correlation Heatmap

sensors 19, 21, 22, 24, 25 are correlated at r > 0.983 — essentially measuring the same thing. sensors 14 & 16 form a second cluster (r = 0.990). sensor_04 is negatively correlated with the high-variance group. You don't need all 52 sensors — a subset of ~15 carries almost all information.

9.

PCA — Dimensionality Reduction

PC1 explains 35.9%, PC2 explains 17.9% — together 53.8%. After 10 components you reach 83.2%. An estimated 14–15 components capture 90% of variance. This confirms massive redundancy: 52 sensors collapse to ~15 independent dimensions driven by a small number of underlying physical factors.

10.

Isolation Forest Anomaly Detection

Trained on hourly top-6 sensor data with 2% contamination parameter. Anomalies (red dots) are not random — they cluster at specific time windows, indicating real abnormal operating periods rather than noise. The model flags ~70 hours across the 5-month window as anomalous.

11.

Anomaly vs Actual Status

RECOVERING hours are flagged as anomalies at 3.3% vs 1.9% for NORMAL — a 1.7× higher rate. With only 7 BROKEN events disappearing in hourly aggregation, this is meaningful validation. The unsupervised model is picking up real signal without ever being told what RECOVERING looks like.
